passages.title: How to spot fake news
passages.text: Misinformation has always existed, but social media has allowed false stories to reach millions of people within hours. There are several steps you can take to identify fake news. Finally, fact-checking websites can help you verify viral claims.

After researching their options, they applied for Portugal's Digital Nomad visa, which requires applicants to prove a minimum monthly income. Since both work remotely, they qualified. They decided to rent in a smaller city initially, as Lisbon has become expensive. To prepare, they also started weekly Portuguese lessons and could already hold a basic conversation.

passages.title: Changing career direction
passages.text: Three years ago, a person was working as an accountant but felt unfulfilled. They had always been interested in sustainability and decided to move into environmental consultancy. First, they enrolled in an evening course in environmental management to get a relevant qualification. Then they started attending industry events to meet professionals already working in sustainability. They also took on pro bono consulting work for small organisations, which gave them real practical experience and case studies. Eventually, they were offered a junior position in a sustainability consultancy. Within two years, they had been promoted twice and were managing their own client accounts.

passages.title: The science of social bonds
passages.text: For decades, social scientists debated whether friendship was primarily a function of personality compatibility or of structural circumstance. Longitudinal research has increasingly supported the latter: the single strongest predictor of friendship formation is not shared values or similar personalities, but propinquity — the tendency of people who are physically or repeatedly in proximity to develop social bonds. We become friends with the people who happen to share our commutes, our workplaces, our classrooms. This finding has uncomfortable implications: much of what we experience as chosen connection is, to a greater degree than we typically acknowledge, the product of circumstances we did not choose. The research does not suggest that deep friendship cannot exist or that personality is irrelevant. Rather, it suggests that propinquity determines the pool of candidates from which deep friendship is then selected. The quality of friendships that develop is influenced by compatibility; the existence of the opportunity is determined by geography and routine.

questions.q: What does longitudinal research identify as the strongest predictor of friendship formation?
options: Shared values and beliefs
Compatible personalities
Propinquity — physical or repeated proximity
Similar educational backgrounds
questions.answer: Propinquity — physical or repeated proximity

questions.q: What uncomfortable implication does the speaker draw from this research?
options: That we do not actually choose our closest friends deliberately
That personality compatibility is the only thing that matters in friendship
That modern technology has destroyed the possibility of genuine friendship
That much of what we experience as chosen connection is partly a product of unchosen circumstances
questions.answer: That much of what we experience as chosen connection is partly a product of unchosen circumstances

questions.q: What role does personality compatibility play according to the passage?
options: It determines whether friendship opportunities arise at all
It influences the quality of friendships once the opportunity exists
It is completely irrelevant to friendship formation
It is more important than propinquity in most cases
questions.answer: It influences the quality of friendships once the opportunity exists

passages.title: Meritocracy and social mobility
passages.text: The meritocratic ideal holds that social outcomes should be determined by individual talent and effort rather than by inherited privilege or social background. As a principle of justice, it has broad appeal across political traditions. The empirical reality, however, is strikingly different from the ideal. Research on intergenerational social mobility consistently shows that the most powerful single predictor of a person's adult income is their parents' income — not their educational attainment, not their measured intelligence, and not their work ethic as assessed by any available metric. Countries that most ardently embrace meritocratic rhetoric — particularly the United States — tend to have lower rates of intergenerational mobility than countries with stronger welfare states and more equalised educational resources, such as the Scandinavian nations. This suggests a troubling possibility: that meritocratic ideology functions partly as a legitimating narrative for inequality, attributing economic outcomes to desert rather than to structural advantage, thereby obscuring the structural changes that would be necessary to create the genuinely equal opportunity the ideology promises.

questions.q: What is the most powerful predictor of adult income according to the research cited?
options: Educational attainment
Measured intelligence
Parents' income
Work ethic and individual effort
questions.answer: Parents' income

questions.q: Which countries tend to have higher rates of social mobility?
options: Countries with strong meritocratic rhetoric like the United States
Countries with stronger welfare states and more equalised educational resources
Countries with the most competitive educational systems
Countries with the highest GDP per capita
questions.answer: Countries with stronger welfare states and more equalised educational resources

questions.q: What troubling function does meritocratic ideology serve according to the passage?
options: It discourages innovation by rewarding conformity
It causes excessive competition that harms wellbeing
It legitimises inequality by attributing outcomes to individual desert rather than structural advantage
It makes education the only path to social advancement
questions.answer: It legitimises inequality by attributing outcomes to individual desert rather than structural advantage

passages.title: Loneliness as a public health crisis
passages.text: The designation of loneliness as a public health crisis rather than a private misfortune reflects a significant shift in how social scientists and health authorities understand the relationship between social connection and biological health. Research over the past two decades has established that chronic loneliness is associated with a range of serious physical health outcomes, including elevated cortisol levels, impaired immune function, disrupted sleep, and increased risk of cardiovascular disease. The effect on mortality is comparable to smoking fifteen cigarettes per day. Despite this evidence, loneliness remains heavily stigmatised, frequently understood as a personal failure or a symptom of introversion rather than as a condition with structural causes. The atomisation of contemporary social life — declining participation in civic organisations, the weakening of neighbourhood ties, the replacement of physical social interaction with its digital simulacra — has created conditions in which loneliness has become structurally normalised even as it has become individually pathologised.

questions.q: What physical health risks are associated with chronic loneliness according to the passage?
options: Only mental health problems such as depression and anxiety
Elevated cortisol, impaired immune function, disrupted sleep, and cardiovascular disease
Primarily digestive problems and reduced energy levels
Mainly increased risk of infectious diseases due to reduced social exposure
questions.answer: Elevated cortisol, impaired immune function, disrupted sleep, and cardiovascular disease

questions.q: How does the mortality effect of loneliness compare according to the passage?
options: It is roughly equivalent to smoking fifteen cigarettes per day
It is less severe than most physical health conditions
It is comparable to being severely overweight
It only affects people over sixty years of age
questions.answer: It is roughly equivalent to smoking fifteen cigarettes per day

questions.q: What structural changes does the passage identify as contributing to normalised loneliness?
options: Increased working hours and economic inequality
Declining civic participation, weakened neighbourhood ties, and replacement of physical interaction with digital substitutes
The breakdown of traditional family structures
Excessive use of pharmaceutical treatments for social anxiety
questions.answer: Declining civic participation, weakened neighbourhood ties, and replacement of physical interaction with digital substitutes

passages.title: Algorithmic decision-making and accountability
passages.text: The increasing deployment of automated decision-making systems in high-stakes domains — credit scoring, recidivism prediction, medical diagnosis, welfare eligibility — raises fundamental questions about accountability that existing legal and regulatory frameworks are poorly equipped to address. When a human decision-maker makes an erroneous or discriminatory decision, there exists at least in principle a chain of accountability: the individual, their institution, and potentially the courts. When the same decision is made by an opaque algorithmic system, this chain becomes considerably more difficult to trace. The 'black box' problem — the inability of even the system's creators to explain precisely why a particular output was generated — undermines the basic requirement of procedural justice that decisions affecting individuals be explicable and contestable. Regulatory responses have focused on explainability requirements, impact assessments, and audit mechanisms, but these remain nascent and unevenly applied across jurisdictions.

questions.q: What does the 'black box' problem refer to in the context of algorithmic systems?
options: The high cost of developing and maintaining AI systems
The inability to explain precisely why a particular output was generated
The tendency of AI systems to favour majority groups
The secrecy around the commercial interests behind AI development
questions.answer: The inability to explain precisely why a particular output was generated

questions.q: What basic requirement of procedural justice does algorithmic opacity undermine?
options: The right to a fair hearing before a judge
The requirement that decisions affecting individuals be explicable and contestable
The right to compensation when an incorrect decision is made
The requirement that decision-makers be qualified professionals
questions.answer: The requirement that decisions affecting individuals be explicable and contestable

questions.q: How does the passage characterise current regulatory responses to algorithmic decision-making?
options: As comprehensive and effectively enforced across all major economies
As overly restrictive, slowing beneficial AI development
As nascent and unevenly applied across jurisdictions
As focused exclusively on preventing racial discrimination
questions.answer: As nascent and unevenly applied across jurisdictions

passages.title: The digital divide beyond access
passages.text: Discussions of the digital divide have historically focused on access — whether individuals have a device and an internet connection. This framing, while important, understates the complexity of the problem. Research on digital inclusion distinguishes between access, skills, and meaningful use. A person may have a smartphone and an internet connection yet lack the digital literacy to evaluate the credibility of online sources, protect their personal data, or use digital tools productively for work or education. This skills dimension of the divide tends to correlate strongly with existing social inequalities: older adults, people with lower levels of formal education, and those in lower-income brackets are systematically disadvantaged on skills measures even when basic access is available. Furthermore, the content dimension matters: the internet as experienced by a person in a high-income country with high digital literacy is qualitatively different from the internet as experienced by someone with limited connectivity and limited skills — not just quantitatively poorer.

questions.q: What three dimensions of digital inclusion does research distinguish?
options: Hardware, software, and connectivity
Access, skills, and meaningful use
Speed, reliability, and affordability
Individual, community, and national levels
questions.answer: Access, skills, and meaningful use

questions.q: Which groups are systematically disadvantaged on digital skills measures?
options: Younger generations who rely too heavily on mobile devices
People in rural areas regardless of their education level
Older adults, people with less formal education, and those in lower-income brackets
People who work in non-technical professions
questions.answer: Older adults, people with less formal education, and those in lower-income brackets

questions.q: What does the passage argue about the internet as experienced by different users?
options: It is essentially the same for all users regardless of skills or location
High-income users use more data but have the same quality of experience
The internet as experienced by a high-literacy user is qualitatively, not just quantitatively, different
Differences in internet experience are determined only by connection speed
questions.answer: The internet as experienced by a high-literacy user is qualitatively, not just quantitatively, different

passages.title: CRISPR and the governance gap
passages.text: The CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing technology has developed faster than the governance frameworks designed to regulate it. When He Jiankui announced in 2018 that he had created the world's first genetically edited human babies — twin girls whose CCR5 gene had been modified in an attempt to confer resistance to HIV — the scientific community responded with near-universal condemnation. His actions were widely characterised as premature, dangerous, and ethically unjustifiable, given that the safety and long-term consequences of germline editing in humans remained unknown. But the incident also exposed the inadequacy of existing regulatory frameworks: He conducted his research in a context where it was not clearly prohibited, and the international scientific community had no enforcement mechanism to prevent it. The governance gap between rapidly developing biotechnology capabilities and the international frameworks to regulate them represents one of the most serious institutional challenges of the current era.

questions.q: What did He Jiankui do that provoked near-universal condemnation?
options: He published research on gene editing without peer review
He created the world's first genetically edited human babies
He modified the genes of patients without their informed consent
He sold gene editing technology to governments without regulatory approval
questions.answer: He created the world's first genetically edited human babies

questions.q: What did the incident expose about existing regulatory frameworks?
options: That they were too restrictive and slowed beneficial research
That He's actions were clearly prohibited but enforcement failed
That the action was not clearly prohibited and there was no international enforcement mechanism
That scientific self-regulation is sufficient to prevent unethical research
questions.answer: That the action was not clearly prohibited and there was no international enforcement mechanism

questions.q: What does the passage describe as one of the most serious institutional challenges of the current era?
options: The rising cost of genetic research and its impact on access
The governance gap between rapidly developing biotechnology capabilities and international frameworks to regulate them
The risk of genetically engineered organisms entering the food supply
The ethical problem of using human subjects in genetic experiments
questions.answer: The governance gap between rapidly developing biotechnology capabilities and international frameworks to regulate them

passages.title: The postcolonial museum debate
passages.text: The debate over the repatriation of cultural objects acquired during colonial periods has intensified significantly in recent years, moving from the margins of academic discourse into mainstream policy discussion. The arguments against repatriation — that objects are better preserved in major international institutions, that they are accessible to a wider international audience, and that ownership should not be determined by historical circumstance — have not disappeared, but they are increasingly contested. Critics point out that the 'universal museum' argument tends to presuppose that the values and interests of the institution holding the object should take precedence over those of the community from which it was taken. The deeper issue is one of epistemic authority: who has the right to interpret and narrate the significance of an object, and for whom? This question cannot be answered by technical conservation arguments alone. Several major European institutions have begun returning specific objects, suggesting that the absolutist defence of existing collections is no longer sustainable.

questions.q: What has happened to the repatriation debate in recent years?
options: It has been resolved by new international law
It has moved from academic margins into mainstream policy discussion
It has been abandoned due to practical difficulties
It has become less politically sensitive as emotions have cooled
questions.answer: It has moved from academic margins into mainstream policy discussion

questions.q: What does the 'universal museum' argument presuppose according to critics?
options: That all cultural objects belong to all of humanity equally
That the values of the holding institution should take precedence over those of the source community
That repatriation would endanger the physical preservation of the objects
That international audiences have more right to access cultural heritage than local ones
questions.answer: That the values of the holding institution should take precedence over those of the source community

questions.q: What is the deeper issue in the repatriation debate according to the passage?
options: Who should bear the financial costs of returning objects
Whether physical preservation standards are higher in Europe than in source countries
Epistemic authority — who has the right to interpret an object and for whom
Whether governments or communities should control cultural property
questions.answer: Epistemic authority — who has the right to interpret an object and for whom

passages.title: Literature and the cultivation of empathy
passages.text: The claim that reading literary fiction cultivates empathy has been both celebrated and contested. Experimental research — most notably a series of studies published in Science by Kidd and Castano — found that reading literary fiction, as distinct from popular fiction or non-fiction, produced measurable improvements in 'theory of mind': the ability to attribute mental states to others and to understand that others' beliefs, desires, and intentions may differ from one's own. The mechanism proposed is immersion in the interior lives of complex, morally ambiguous characters — something that literary fiction provides and that other narrative forms do less reliably. Critics of this research point to replication difficulties and question whether laboratory-measured improvements in theory of mind translate to real-world empathetic behaviour. Nevertheless, the broader claim — that sustained engagement with serious literature changes how readers understand other people's inner lives — has sufficient support to be taken seriously as a basis for arguments about the social value of literary culture.

questions.q: What did the research by Kidd and Castano find about reading literary fiction?
options: It improved vocabulary and grammatical accuracy significantly
It produced measurable improvements in theory of mind
It reduced anxiety and improved mental health outcomes
It was less engaging than popular fiction but more educational
questions.answer: It produced measurable improvements in theory of mind

questions.q: What mechanism does the research propose for the empathy-building effect of literary fiction?
options: Exposure to historically and culturally diverse situations
Immersion in the interior lives of complex, morally ambiguous characters
The challenge of understanding complex narrative structures
Identification with heroic characters who overcome adversity
questions.answer: Immersion in the interior lives of complex, morally ambiguous characters

questions.q: What criticism is raised against this research?
options: The study used only students, not a representative sample
Literary fiction readers were already more empathetic before the study
There are replication difficulties and questions about whether results translate to real-world behaviour
The definition of literary fiction used was too broad to be meaningful
questions.answer: There are replication difficulties and questions about whether results translate to real-world behaviour

passages.title: The economics of art and cultural value
passages.text: There is a persistent tension between the market valuation of art and its cultural valuation, and the two do not consistently correlate. A painting may command tens of millions at auction while the artist who painted it died in poverty; conversely, works of immense cultural significance — particularly in folk, community, and non-Western traditions — may have negligible market value. The art market as it currently operates is not primarily a mechanism for allocating resources to the production of culturally valuable art; it functions more as a vehicle for storing and transferring wealth among the wealthy, with art's cultural status providing the social legitimacy that makes this function acceptable. This does not mean that markets produce no culturally valuable art — they demonstrably do. But it does mean that market success and cultural value are distinct and imperfectly correlated phenomena, and that policy arguments for arts funding based solely on economic returns systematically undervalue what cultural production actually contributes to a society.

questions.q: What does the passage say about the relationship between market valuation and cultural valuation of art?
options: They are highly correlated — expensive art is culturally significant
They do not consistently correlate with each other
Market valuation is always higher than cultural valuation
Cultural valuation is determined by market success over time
questions.answer: They do not consistently correlate with each other

questions.q: How does the passage characterise the primary function of the art market?
options: As a mechanism for allocating resources to culturally valuable art production
As a vehicle for storing and transferring wealth, legitimised by cultural status
As a democratic system that allows any artwork to reach its true value
As a system designed to support living artists in competitive economies
questions.answer: As a vehicle for storing and transferring wealth, legitimised by cultural status

questions.q: What does the passage argue about policy arguments for arts funding based on economic returns?
options: They are the most persuasive basis for public arts investment
They accurately capture the full value of cultural production
They systematically undervalue what cultural production actually contributes to society
They are only appropriate for commercial cultural sectors like film and music
questions.answer: They systematically undervalue what cultural production actually contributes to society

passages.title: The gig economy and labour law
passages.text: The legal classification of platform workers — the drivers, delivery couriers, and domestic service providers who work through apps — as independent contractors rather than employees has been one of the defining labour law controversies of the past decade. For the platforms, contractor classification avoids the substantial costs associated with employment: minimum wage obligations, sick pay, pension contributions, and liability for workplace accidents. For workers, the classification denies access to these protections while often imposing the same practical constraints as employment — specific hours, set rates, performance monitoring, and the ever-present threat of deactivation. Courts in multiple jurisdictions have rejected the contractor classification as a legal fiction that obscures a fundamentally subordinate employment relationship. The UK Supreme Court's 2021 ruling that Uber drivers were workers — not employees, but a recognised intermediate category with certain protections — was particularly significant, combining legal recognition of algorithmic control with practical protection for a large and precarious workforce.

questions.q: Why do platforms prefer to classify workers as independent contractors?
options: Because contractors have more flexibility and prefer this arrangement
To avoid the substantial costs associated with employment — minimum wage, sick pay, pensions, liability
Because employment law does not apply to technology companies
Because the work is genuinely independent and project-based
questions.answer: To avoid the substantial costs associated with employment — minimum wage, sick pay, pensions, liability

questions.q: What did the UK Supreme Court's 2021 Uber ruling establish?
options: That Uber drivers were full employees entitled to all employment rights
That Uber could classify all drivers as contractors indefinitely
That Uber drivers were workers — an intermediate category with certain protections
That labour law did not apply to platform-based work
questions.answer: That Uber drivers were workers — an intermediate category with certain protections

questions.q: What contradiction does the passage identify in the contractor classification?
options: Workers earn more as contractors but have less job security
Contractors legally receive fewer protections despite often facing the same practical constraints as employees
Contractor status is beneficial for high-income workers but harmful for lower-income ones
The classification varies so much between countries that it creates legal confusion
questions.answer: Contractors legally receive fewer protections despite often facing the same practical constraints as employees

passages.title: Carbon pricing and climate policy
passages.text: Carbon pricing — placing a direct cost on greenhouse gas emissions — is broadly recognised by economists as the most efficient mechanism for reducing emissions, yet it remains politically difficult to implement at sufficient scale. The economic logic is straightforward: if emitting carbon has no price, markets will overproduce it; if it has a price that reflects the social cost of its consequences, emitters will have an incentive to reduce emissions. There are two main mechanisms: a carbon tax, which sets the price directly, and a cap-and-trade system, which sets the quantity of permissible emissions and allows the market to determine the price. Both have been implemented in various jurisdictions with mixed results. The political obstacles are significant: carbon pricing increases the cost of energy, disproportionately affecting lower-income households who spend a larger share of their income on fuel. Without complementary redistribution measures, carbon pricing can be socially regressive even while being environmentally effective — a combination that generates predictable political resistance.

questions.q: What is the economic logic behind carbon pricing?
options: It funds renewable energy research through government revenue
If emitting carbon has a price reflecting its social cost, emitters have an incentive to reduce emissions
It makes imported goods from high-emission countries more expensive
It allows governments to cap total emissions through direct regulation
questions.answer: If emitting carbon has a price reflecting its social cost, emitters have an incentive to reduce emissions

questions.q: What is the difference between a carbon tax and a cap-and-trade system?
options: A carbon tax applies only to industry; cap-and-trade applies to consumers
A carbon tax sets the price directly; cap-and-trade sets the quantity and lets the market determine the price
Cap-and-trade is used only in developed countries; carbon taxes in developing ones
A carbon tax is voluntary; cap-and-trade is legally mandatory
questions.answer: A carbon tax sets the price directly; cap-and-trade sets the quantity and lets the market determine the price

questions.q: Why can carbon pricing be socially regressive?
options: Because it increases costs for businesses that employ the poorest workers
Because it increases energy costs, disproportionately affecting lower-income households who spend more of their income on fuel
Because it benefits large corporations that can afford clean technology
Because the revenue from carbon taxes is often captured by wealthy investors
questions.answer: Because it increases energy costs, disproportionately affecting lower-income households who spend more of their income on fuel

passages.title: Startup failure and survivor bias
passages.text: The popular narrative surrounding entrepreneurship is shaped disproportionately by exceptional successes — the garage startups that became global corporations, the first-time founders who achieved billion-dollar valuations. This narrative distorts understanding of entrepreneurship in a systematic way: by focusing on the survivors, it renders invisible the vastly larger number of companies that attempted the same things and failed. This is survivor bias, and it affects not only public perception but the practical advice that entrepreneurs receive. If we observe that successful founders shared certain characteristics — high risk tolerance, intense focus, willingness to pivot — we cannot conclude that these characteristics caused success unless we also establish that unsuccessful founders lacked them. In most cases, they did not: the distinguishing factor was not character but circumstance, market timing, and what economists call 'luck' — the confluence of factors outside any individual's control. This does not mean effort and skill are irrelevant; it means their contribution to outcomes is smaller than the survivor narrative suggests.

questions.q: What is survivor bias in the context of entrepreneurship?
options: The tendency for experienced entrepreneurs to mentor younger ones
The distortion caused by studying successful companies while rendering unsuccessful ones invisible
The advantage that serial entrepreneurs have over first-time founders
The belief that persistence always leads to eventual success
questions.answer: The distortion caused by studying successful companies while rendering unsuccessful ones invisible

questions.q: What logical problem does the passage identify in observing characteristics of successful founders?
options: Successful founders are too few in number to draw reliable conclusions
We cannot conclude characteristics caused success without establishing that unsuccessful founders lacked them
The characteristics observed change too much over time to be useful
Success characteristics are too culturally specific to generalise
questions.answer: We cannot conclude characteristics caused success without establishing that unsuccessful founders lacked them

questions.q: What does the passage say about the role of luck in entrepreneurial outcomes?
options: Luck is completely separate from skill and cannot be cultivated
Luck is the primary factor — skill and effort are essentially irrelevant
Luck — the confluence of uncontrollable factors — contributes more to outcomes than the survivor narrative suggests
Successful entrepreneurs create their own luck through preparation
questions.answer: Luck — the confluence of uncontrollable factors — contributes more to outcomes than the survivor narrative suggests

passages.title: Democratic backsliding from within
passages.text: The most significant threat to democracy in the early twenty-first century has not come from external military force or dramatic coup d'état, but from the incremental erosion of democratic norms and institutions by leaders who were themselves democratically elected. Political scientists call this process democratic backsliding, and its characteristic feature is that it operates through democratic mechanisms rather than against them: elections are held, courts continue to function, and parliaments remain in session, but each of these institutions is gradually weakened, packed with loyalists, or delegitimised in public discourse. The process typically begins with attacks on institutions perceived as obstacles — independent courts, free media, autonomous electoral commissions — framed as necessary corrections to elite bias or institutional corruption. By the time the damage is severe, the very institutions required to resist and reverse it have been compromised. Reversing democratic backsliding has proven consistently more difficult than preventing it, which places an asymmetric burden on democratic publics: the cost of vigilance is ongoing, but the cost of its absence can be irreversible.

questions.q: What distinguishes democratic backsliding from other threats to democracy?
options: It is caused by foreign interference rather than domestic actors
It operates through democratic mechanisms rather than against them
It always involves the suspension of elections and constitutional rights
It is driven by economic crisis rather than political ambition
questions.answer: It operates through democratic mechanisms rather than against them

questions.q: What is the typical first target of democratic backsliding?
options: Local government and municipal institutions
The military and security services
Institutions perceived as obstacles — independent courts, free media, electoral commissions
Academic institutions and universities
questions.answer: Institutions perceived as obstacles — independent courts, free media, electoral commissions

questions.q: What asymmetric burden does the passage say falls on democratic publics?
options: They must fund democratic institutions without receiving direct benefits
The cost of vigilance is ongoing, but the cost of its absence can be irreversible
They must participate in elections even when their preferred candidates are excluded
Democratic publics bear the costs of democratic governance while elites capture the benefits
questions.answer: The cost of vigilance is ongoing, but the cost of its absence can be irreversible

passages.title: The collective action problem of climate change
passages.text: Climate change presents one of the most intractable collective action problems in human history: the costs of reducing emissions fall on specific actors in the present, while the benefits of mitigation accrue to diffuse populations over long timescales, many of whom have not yet been born. This temporal and distributional mismatch is compounded by the structure of international relations, which remains organised around sovereign nation-states with no supranational authority capable of compelling compliance. Each state has an incentive to free-ride on the emissions reductions of others, enjoying the benefits of a stabilised climate without bearing the full costs of contributing to it. International climate agreements address this through a combination of national commitments, transparency mechanisms, and increasingly, trade measures that impose costs on high-emission imports. But the fundamental enforcement problem — that international law depends on voluntary compliance — has not been resolved, and the gap between stated commitments and actual emissions trajectories in most major economies remains substantial.

questions.q: What makes climate change a difficult collective action problem?
options: The scientific complexity of climate modelling makes agreement impossible
The costs of emission reduction fall on present actors while benefits accrue to diffuse future populations
The technology for reducing emissions does not yet exist at sufficient scale
Climate change affects different countries so differently that agreement on solutions is impossible
questions.answer: The costs of emission reduction fall on present actors while benefits accrue to diffuse future populations

questions.q: What is the 'free-rider' incentive in international climate action?
options: The incentive to develop green technology and sell it to other countries
Each state's incentive to enjoy climate benefits without bearing the full costs of contributing to them
The incentive for wealthy countries to pay developing countries to reduce their emissions
The advantage that countries gain from early adoption of clean energy technology
questions.answer: Each state's incentive to enjoy climate benefits without bearing the full costs of contributing to them

questions.q: What fundamental problem in international climate agreements remains unresolved?
options: The lack of a scientific consensus on the required level of emission reductions
The impossibility of monitoring actual emissions in real time
International law depends on voluntary compliance — there is no enforcement mechanism
Developing countries cannot afford the transition to clean energy without financial support
questions.answer: International law depends on voluntary compliance — there is no enforcement mechanism

passages.title: The ethics of humanitarian intervention
passages.text: The 'Responsibility to Protect' (R2P) doctrine, adopted by the United Nations in 2005, sought to establish a new norm in international relations: that state sovereignty is not an absolute shield against external intervention when a government is committing or failing to prevent mass atrocities against its own population. The doctrine represented a significant conceptual shift, reframing sovereignty as conditional — contingent on the fulfilment of responsibilities toward citizens rather than as an unconditional right. In practice, the implementation of R2P has been deeply inconsistent, reflecting the political interests and relationships of the permanent members of the UN Security Council rather than any principled application of the doctrine. Interventions have occurred where they were strategically convenient for major powers; they have been blocked where they were not. This inconsistency is itself damaging: a norm that is selectively applied not only fails to protect those it claims to protect but actively delegitimises the institutions that invoke it.

questions.q: What did the Responsibility to Protect doctrine establish?
options: That all nations have an absolute right to sovereignty regardless of their treatment of citizens
That sovereignty is conditional — dependent on fulfilling responsibilities toward citizens
That the UN Security Council has the right to intervene in any domestic conflict
That international courts can prosecute any government for human rights violations
questions.answer: That sovereignty is conditional — dependent on fulfilling responsibilities toward citizens

questions.q: What has determined the actual implementation of R2P in practice?
options: A consistent principled application of the doctrine by the UN
The severity and scale of human rights violations in each case
The political interests and relationships of permanent Security Council members
The willingness of regional organisations to lead intervention efforts
questions.answer: The political interests and relationships of permanent Security Council members

questions.q: Why does the passage say selective application of R2P is itself damaging?
options: Because it causes military interventions to be more costly and dangerous
Because it makes future international agreements on human rights impossible
Because a norm selectively applied fails those it claims to protect and delegitimises the institutions invoking it
Because it gives permanent Security Council members too much power
questions.answer: Because a norm selectively applied fails those it claims to protect and delegitimises the institutions invoking it

passages.title: The neuroscience of creativity and the default mode network
passages.text: The dominant cognitive model of the early twenty-first century positioned focused, analytical attention as the paradigmatic form of productive mental activity. Work environments, educational systems, and productivity culture were all organised around the principle that sustained, undistracted concentration is the condition under which valuable cognitive work occurs. Neuroscientific research has complicated this picture significantly. The Default Mode Network — a set of brain regions including the medial prefrontal cortex, the posterior cingulate cortex, and the temporoparietal junction — was long dismissed as the brain's resting state. It is now understood to be among the most metabolically active networks in the brain during undirected mental states, and to be critically implicated in autobiographical memory, theory of mind, prospective thought, and — most relevantly for creativity — the spontaneous generation of novel associations between conceptually distant domains. The practical implication is counterintuitive: the conditions most conducive to creative insight are precisely the conditions that contemporary work culture most systematically eliminates — boredom, undirected reverie, and the perceptual freedom of an undemanding environment.

questions.q: What was the earlier scientific understanding of the Default Mode Network?
options: That it was the primary network for analytical and focused thought
That it was the brain's resting state — essentially inactive during valuable cognitive work
That it was responsible for emotional regulation and stress response
That it was active only during sleep and deep meditation
questions.answer: That it was the brain's resting state — essentially inactive during valuable cognitive work

questions.q: What cognitive functions is the Default Mode Network now understood to support?
options: Language processing, mathematical reasoning, and spatial navigation
Autobiographical memory, theory of mind, prospective thought, and novel association generation
Motor control, sensory perception, and reaction time
Executive function, working memory, and decision-making under pressure
questions.answer: Autobiographical memory, theory of mind, prospective thought, and novel association generation

questions.q: What is the counterintuitive practical implication of this research?
options: Focused work is more productive than most people assume
The conditions most conducive to creativity are precisely those contemporary work culture eliminates
Creativity requires formal training that most education systems do not provide
The most creative people work longer hours than their less creative counterparts
questions.answer: The conditions most conducive to creativity are precisely those contemporary work culture eliminates

passages.title: The biology of ageing and the prospect of life extension
passages.text: Scientific understanding of the biological mechanisms of ageing has advanced dramatically over the past two decades, to the point where the research community no longer treats ageing as an immutable feature of biological existence. The hallmarks of ageing — a framework introduced in a landmark 2013 paper and updated in 2023 — identifies a set of cellular and molecular processes that collectively produce the deterioration associated with ageing: genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, deregulated nutrient sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, and altered intercellular communication. Multiple interventions targeting these hallmarks have extended healthy lifespan in animal models. The translation of these findings to human applications faces significant challenges, including the longer timescales required for human trials and the complexity of interactions between ageing mechanisms in organisms far more complex than laboratory mice. Nevertheless, a growing number of biotechnology companies are pursuing human longevity interventions, and the question has shifted from whether human lifespan extension is theoretically possible to whether it is practically achievable and ethically desirable.

questions.q: What shift has occurred in how the research community views ageing?
options: Ageing is increasingly understood as a disease requiring medical treatment
The community no longer treats ageing as an immutable feature of biological existence
Researchers have concluded that genetic modification is the only solution to ageing
The scientific consensus now holds that ageing cannot be meaningfully slowed
questions.answer: The community no longer treats ageing as an immutable feature of biological existence

questions.q: What does the 'hallmarks of ageing' framework identify?
options: The lifestyle factors most associated with early death
A set of cellular and molecular processes that collectively produce age-related deterioration
The genetic mutations responsible for premature ageing diseases
The environmental factors that accelerate biological ageing
questions.answer: A set of cellular and molecular processes that collectively produce age-related deterioration

questions.q: What challenge does translating animal model findings to humans present?
options: Humans are unwilling to participate in longevity research trials
The ethical problems of life extension are too great to permit human trials
The longer timescales required for human trials and the greater complexity of human biology
Longevity interventions are too expensive to test in human populations
questions.answer: The longer timescales required for human trials and the greater complexity of human biology

passages.title: The hard problem of consciousness and artificial minds
passages.text: The question of whether artificial systems can be conscious — and, if so, how we could know — is among the most consequential and least tractable philosophical questions raised by the development of advanced AI. The difficulty is not primarily technical but conceptual. Philosopher David Chalmers distinguished between the 'easy' problems of consciousness — explaining the neural and computational mechanisms underlying cognitive functions such as attention, memory, and perception — and the 'hard' problem: explaining why these mechanisms are accompanied by subjective experience at all, why there is something it is like to be a conscious entity rather than simply a very sophisticated information-processing system operating in the dark. Current AI systems — including the most capable large language models — are, at minimum, sophisticated information processors that generate outputs indistinguishable in many contexts from conscious human responses. Whether this functional competence is accompanied by any form of inner experience is a question that cannot be resolved by behavioural evidence alone, precisely because the hard problem resists any purely functional answer. This creates genuine uncertainty about the moral status of advanced AI systems that existing ethical frameworks are inadequately equipped to address.

questions.q: What does Chalmers distinguish between in his account of consciousness?
options: Artificial and natural consciousness
The easy problems — explaining cognitive mechanisms — and the hard problem — explaining subjective experience
Conscious and unconscious mental processes
The computational and the biological bases of thought
questions.answer: The easy problems — explaining cognitive mechanisms — and the hard problem — explaining subjective experience

questions.q: Why cannot behavioural evidence resolve the question of AI consciousness?
options: Behaviour is too complex to measure reliably in AI systems
Because the hard problem resists any purely functional answer
Because AI behaviour is always scripted and therefore not genuine
Because humans are biased in their interpretation of AI behaviour
questions.answer: Because the hard problem resists any purely functional answer

questions.q: What genuine uncertainty does this create according to the passage?
options: Whether AI systems can be trusted to make accurate decisions
Whether AI systems will eventually become physically dangerous
About the moral status of advanced AI systems, which existing ethical frameworks cannot adequately address
Whether AI development should continue given the unknown risks
questions.answer: About the moral status of advanced AI systems, which existing ethical frameworks cannot adequately address

passages.title: Democratic backsliding and the erosion of constitutional norms
passages.text: Democratic backsliding — the gradual erosion of democratic institutions, norms, and practices — has emerged as one of the most pressing concerns in comparative politics. Unlike the abrupt military coups of the twentieth century, contemporary democratic erosion typically occurs incrementally, through the accumulation of individually defensible measures that collectively undermine the checks and balances on executive power. Incumbents exploit the formal mechanisms of democracy — electoral majorities, legislative procedures, judicial appointments — to entrench their hold on power while maintaining the outward appearance of democratic legitimacy. The judiciary is typically targeted first: constitutional courts are packed with loyalists, tenure protections are weakened, and independent prosecutors are removed. Electoral bodies follow: redistricting is manipulated, voter eligibility rules are tightened for communities likely to oppose the government, and media regulation is used to disadvantage opposition voices. The process is most insidious precisely because it proceeds legally, making it difficult for citizens and international actors to identify a clear moment at which democratic governance has been extinguished. Scholars have coined the term 'constitutional hardball' to describe the use of technically legal but constitutionally questionable tactics that stretch the boundaries of accepted political conduct. The cumulative effect, however, is the systematic dismantling of the accountability mechanisms that distinguish democracy from competitive authoritarianism.

questions.q: How does contemporary democratic backsliding differ from earlier forms of democratic collapse?
options: It involves foreign interference rather than domestic actors
It occurs gradually through the accumulation of individually defensible measures rather than through sudden coups
It is led by military forces rather than elected officials
It primarily affects economic rather than political institutions
questions.answer: It occurs gradually through the accumulation of individually defensible measures rather than through sudden coups

questions.q: Why does the passage describe the process of democratic backsliding as 'most insidious'?
options: Because it is supported by large sections of the population
Because it targets economic institutions rather than political ones
Because it proceeds legally, making it difficult to identify a clear moment of democratic collapse
Because it is coordinated by external actors rather than domestic politicians
questions.answer: Because it proceeds legally, making it difficult to identify a clear moment of democratic collapse

questions.q: What does the term 'constitutional hardball' refer to, as used in the passage?
options: Violent confrontations between political parties over constitutional changes
The use of technically legal but constitutionally questionable tactics that stretch acceptable political conduct
The practice of holding referendums on constitutional amendments
The strategy of challenging electoral results through the court system
questions.answer: The use of technically legal but constitutionally questionable tactics that stretch acceptable political conduct

passages.title: Populism, rhetoric, and the politics of resentment
passages.text: Populism is best understood not as an ideology in the conventional sense but as a political logic — a way of framing political conflict as a moral struggle between a virtuous, homogeneous 'people' and a corrupt, self-serving 'elite'. This Manichean vision, which simplifies complex social realities into a binary opposition, has proven remarkably durable across diverse cultural and political contexts, from Latin American left-wing movements to European right-wing nationalist parties. The rhetorical power of populism derives partly from its capacity to give voice to legitimate grievances — economic insecurity, cultural displacement, distrust of institutions — while channelling them toward scapegoating rather than structural reform. Populist leaders exploit the gap between formal democratic procedures and the lived experience of democratic exclusion, presenting themselves as the authentic embodiment of popular will in opposition to the procedural constraints of liberal constitutionalism. This creates an inherent tension between populism and representative democracy: while populists invoke the language of democratic legitimacy, their hostility to institutional constraints, media scrutiny, and judicial independence tends to corrode the very mechanisms by which democratic accountability is maintained. Analysts have distinguished between a 'thin' populism — the core anti-establishment appeal — and the varying 'thick' ideological content with which it is combined in different contexts, whether left-wing redistributionism, right-wing nativism, or technocratic efficiency discourse.

questions.q: How does the passage define populism?
options: As a left-wing political ideology concerned with economic redistribution
As a political logic that frames conflict as a moral struggle between the people and a corrupt elite
As a form of nationalism that prioritises cultural homogeneity
As a technocratic approach to governance that bypasses democratic procedures
questions.answer: As a political logic that frames conflict as a moral struggle between the people and a corrupt elite

questions.q: According to the passage, what is the source of populism's rhetorical power?
options: Its ability to offer concrete policy solutions to economic problems
Its association with charismatic leadership and mass mobilisation
Its capacity to voice legitimate grievances while channelling them toward scapegoating rather than reform
Its use of sophisticated media strategies to reach disillusioned voters
questions.answer: Its capacity to voice legitimate grievances while channelling them toward scapegoating rather than reform

questions.q: What distinction do analysts draw between 'thin' and 'thick' populism?
options: Between populism in wealthy and developing countries
Between popular and elite forms of political mobilisation
Between the core anti-establishment appeal and the varying ideological content combined with it
Between democratic and authoritarian forms of populist governance
questions.answer: Between the core anti-establishment appeal and the varying ideological content combined with it

passages.title: The separation of powers and the rule of law
passages.text: The doctrine of the separation of powers — the institutional division of government authority among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches — was conceived as a structural safeguard against the concentration of power in any single set of hands. Montesquieu's classical formulation, which influenced the framers of the American constitution and countless subsequent constitutional designers, held that liberty could only be preserved when the power to make laws, the power to execute them, and the power to adjudicate disputes were distributed among distinct and mutually checking institutions. In practice, no modern democracy has achieved a pure separation; what constitutional systems aspire to instead is a system of checks and balances in which each branch possesses tools to constrain the others. The independence of the judiciary is particularly crucial: courts must be able to review executive action for legality and assess whether legislation conforms to constitutional requirements without fear of political retribution. The rule of law — the principle that all persons and institutions, including the government itself, are accountable to laws that are publicly promulgated, equally enforced, and independently adjudicated — depends fundamentally on this judicial independence. Where courts are subordinated to executive preferences, the rule of law collapses into the rule of men, and the formal procedures of democracy become instruments of power rather than constraints upon it. The formal subjunctive, still common in legal English, reflects this culture of institutional obligation: it is essential that every constitutional actor remain within the boundaries of their constitutionally assigned authority.

questions.q: What was the original purpose of the doctrine of the separation of powers?
options: To ensure that all citizens have equal representation in government
To serve as a structural safeguard against the concentration of power in any single institution
To create an efficient administrative system for a large state
To protect the rights of minority groups against majority rule
questions.answer: To serve as a structural safeguard against the concentration of power in any single institution

questions.q: Why is judicial independence described as 'particularly crucial' in the passage?
options: Because judges have greater technical expertise than legislators or executives
Because courts must be able to review executive and legislative action without fear of political retribution
Because judicial appointments represent the most democratic part of the constitutional system
Because judicial decisions are immune from public scrutiny and criticism
questions.answer: Because courts must be able to review executive and legislative action without fear of political retribution

questions.q: What does the passage say happens when courts are subordinated to executive preferences?
options: The legislative process becomes more efficient and effective
The rule of law collapses into the rule of men and democracy's formal procedures become instruments of power
Citizens lose confidence in elections as a mechanism for changing government
The judicial branch is eventually abolished and replaced by executive agencies
questions.answer: The rule of law collapses into the rule of men and democracy's formal procedures become instruments of power

passages.title: The nature of moral knowledge and ethical relativism
passages.text: The question of whether moral knowledge is possible in the same sense as scientific or mathematical knowledge is among the most contested in philosophy. Moral realists hold that there are objective moral facts — facts about what is right, wrong, good, or evil — that exist independently of what any individual or culture believes. On this view, moral claims can be true or false in precisely the way that empirical claims can, and moral progress consists in bringing our beliefs into better alignment with these objective facts. Moral relativists, by contrast, maintain that moral standards are culturally contingent: what is right in one society or historical period may be wrong in another, and there is no neutral standpoint from which one culture's moral framework can be judged superior to another's. This position has the virtue of appearing tolerant and non-imperialist, but it generates a troubling implication: if morality is merely a function of cultural consensus, then the moral reforms achieved by figures such as Wilberforce or Mandela — who challenged the prevailing moral consensus of their times — were not moral improvements at all but simply changes in preference. A third position, moral constructivism, attempts to navigate between these extremes by grounding moral norms in the procedures of rational deliberation rather than in external facts or cultural consensus. Kantian constructivism, for instance, holds that the categorical imperative is not discovered but constructed through the application of pure practical reason, generating norms that are both rationally necessary and universally binding.

questions.q: What is the position of moral realists, as described in the passage?
options: That moral standards vary between cultures and historical periods
That there are objective moral facts that exist independently of individual or cultural belief
That moral norms are constructed through rational deliberation and social agreement
That moral progress is impossible because values are fundamentally subjective
questions.answer: That there are objective moral facts that exist independently of individual or cultural belief

questions.q: What troubling implication does the passage identify in moral relativism?
options: That it makes cross-cultural communication about moral issues impossible
That it implies moral reforms like those of Wilberforce and Mandela were not genuine improvements
That it provides no basis for resolving disputes within a single culture
That it is logically self-refuting because it claims to be universally true
questions.answer: That it implies moral reforms like those of Wilberforce and Mandela were not genuine improvements

questions.q: How does moral constructivism differ from both realism and relativism?
options: It accepts cultural relativism while insisting that some cultures are morally superior to others
It grounds moral norms in rational deliberation rather than in external facts or cultural consensus
It rejects the possibility of moral knowledge entirely in favour of aesthetic judgement
It treats moral norms as divine commands that cannot be evaluated by human reason
questions.answer: It grounds moral norms in rational deliberation rather than in external facts or cultural consensus

passages.title: Free will, determinism, and moral responsibility
passages.text: The problem of free will — whether human beings are genuinely capable of acting otherwise than they do — bears directly on our practices of praise, blame, reward, and punishment. Hard determinists argue that every human action is the inevitable product of prior causes — genetic predispositions, environmental conditioning, neurological states — and that, because these causes themselves are not chosen, genuine moral responsibility is an illusion. If determinism is true, they contend, then punishing wrongdoers for their actions is as irrational as blaming a stone for falling. Libertarian free will theorists respond that this conclusion is unacceptable and that human beings possess a form of agency — the capacity for genuinely undetermined choice — that transcends the causal order described by physics. Compatibilists, who represent the majority position among professional philosophers, reject both horns of this dilemma. They argue that the sense of freedom required for moral responsibility does not require the ability to have done otherwise in the metaphysical sense that hard determinists target; it requires only that action flow from the agent's own reasons, desires, and deliberative processes without external coercion or internal compulsion. On the compatibilist view, a person who acts freely when they act on the basis of their own values, even if those values were themselves causally determined. This position preserves the coherence of moral responsibility while accommodating the scientific picture of the world as a causally closed system.

questions.q: What is the position of hard determinists on moral responsibility?
options: That moral responsibility requires libertarian free will
That moral responsibility is preserved as long as actions flow from an agent's own desires
That genuine moral responsibility is an illusion because every action is determined by prior causes
That moral responsibility depends on the agent's ability to predict the consequences of their actions
questions.answer: That genuine moral responsibility is an illusion because every action is determined by prior causes

questions.q: What distinguishes compatibilism from hard determinism and libertarian free will?
options: Compatibilists deny that determinism is scientifically well-supported
Compatibilists argue that free will requires only that action flow from one's own reasons without coercion, not metaphysical underdetermination
Compatibilists hold that free will and determinism are equally false
Compatibilists believe that free will is restricted to exceptional individuals
questions.answer: Compatibilists argue that free will requires only that action flow from one's own reasons without coercion, not metaphysical underdetermination

questions.q: What analogy do hard determinists use to illustrate their view, according to the passage?
options: Comparing human choices to the programmed outputs of a computer
Arguing that punishing wrongdoers is as irrational as blaming a stone for falling
Suggesting that free will is a social fiction maintained for purposes of social control
Claiming that neuroscience has definitively disproved the existence of conscious agency
questions.answer: Arguing that punishing wrongdoers is as irrational as blaming a stone for falling

passages.title: Utilitarianism and its critics
passages.text: Utilitarianism, the ethical theory associated with Jeremy Bentham and developed by John Stuart Mill, holds that the morally right action in any situation is the one that produces the greatest aggregate welfare for the greatest number of people affected. Its appeal lies in its democratic spirit — every individual's welfare counts equally — and its apparent alignment with our intuition that suffering is bad and wellbeing is good. Critics, however, have identified a series of powerful objections. The first concerns justice: classical utilitarianism can, in principle, justify the punishment of an innocent person if doing so would produce sufficient aggregate benefit, or the exploitation of a minority for the majority's advantage. This seems to violate a fundamental moral intuition that individuals possess rights that cannot be traded off against aggregate calculations. The second objection concerns integrity: utilitarian demands may require us to abandon our deepest personal commitments whenever doing so would produce marginally greater aggregate welfare, threatening the stable sense of self that meaningful human life requires. Bernard Williams argued that a moral theory that could require a pacifist to commit an act of violence to prevent slightly greater violence committed by others fails to respect the agent's right to be the author of their own moral history. Preference utilitarianism, associated with Peter Singer, attempts to address some of these concerns by focusing on the satisfaction of informed preferences rather than raw sensations of pleasure and pain, but it generates its own counterintuitive implications when applied to questions of animal welfare and population ethics.

questions.q: What is the core principle of utilitarianism as described in the passage?
options: That individuals have inviolable rights that cannot be overridden by collective welfare calculations
That the morally right action is the one that produces the greatest aggregate welfare for the greatest number
That moral obligations are derived from universally applicable rational principles
That virtuous character traits are the foundation of moral behaviour
questions.answer: That the morally right action is the one that produces the greatest aggregate welfare for the greatest number

questions.q: What is the 'integrity objection' to utilitarianism?
options: That it fails to account for the distribution of welfare across different groups
That it cannot be practically applied because welfare is impossible to measure accurately
That utilitarian demands may require abandoning one's deepest commitments for marginal aggregate gains, threatening personal integrity
That it privileges present over future generations in its welfare calculations
questions.answer: That utilitarian demands may require abandoning one's deepest commitments for marginal aggregate gains, threatening personal integrity

questions.q: How does preference utilitarianism differ from classical utilitarianism?
options: It focuses on the satisfaction of informed preferences rather than raw sensations of pleasure and pain
It restricts the circle of moral concern to human beings only
It requires equal distribution of resources rather than maximisation of aggregate welfare
It grounds moral obligations in social contract rather than welfare maximisation
questions.answer: It focuses on the satisfaction of informed preferences rather than raw sensations of pleasure and pain

passages.title: The replication crisis and the reform of scientific practice
passages.text: The replication crisis — the widespread failure to reproduce the results of previously published studies — has shaken confidence in several fields of empirical science, most prominently social psychology, nutrition research, and medicine. The crisis became widely visible when a large-scale collaborative project, the Reproducibility Project, attempted to replicate one hundred published psychology studies and found that fewer than half produced results consistent with the originals. The roots of the problem lie in a cluster of incentive structures and methodological practices that systematically bias the scientific literature toward positive findings. Publication bias — the tendency of journals to accept studies that report significant results while rejecting those that do not — creates a distorted picture of the evidence base. Researchers respond to these incentives through practices that have been collectively labelled 'questionable research practices': selectively reporting dependent variables, continuing data collection until a significant result is obtained (p-hacking), and presenting exploratory analyses as if they were confirmatory hypotheses (HARKing — Hypothesising After Results are Known). The cumulative effect is a scientific literature populated with findings that are not robust, not replicable, and not a reliable guide to truth. Reform efforts have focused on pre-registration — requiring researchers to register their hypotheses, methods, and analysis plan before data collection begins — open data sharing, and the establishment of replication studies as a legitimate and publishable contribution to scientific knowledge.

questions.q: What did the Reproducibility Project find when it attempted to replicate one hundred psychology studies?
options: That all one hundred studies produced identical results to the originals
That approximately half the studies produced results consistent with the originals
That fewer than half the studies produced results consistent with the originals
That the majority of studies had been deliberately falsified by their original authors
questions.answer: That fewer than half the studies produced results consistent with the originals

questions.q: What is 'p-hacking' as described in the passage?
options: The practice of falsifying statistical data in published research
Continuing data collection until a significant result is obtained to exploit chance fluctuations
Publishing the same study multiple times in different journals
Using computer algorithms to generate artificially significant findings
questions.answer: Continuing data collection until a significant result is obtained to exploit chance fluctuations

questions.q: What is pre-registration and why has it been proposed as a reform?
options: The requirement to obtain ethical approval before conducting research involving human subjects
The requirement to register hypotheses, methods, and analysis plans before data collection to prevent post-hoc rationalisation
The practice of sharing raw data with other researchers before submitting findings for publication
The requirement to conduct a pilot study before undertaking a full-scale investigation
questions.answer: The requirement to register hypotheses, methods, and analysis plans before data collection to prevent post-hoc rationalisation

passages.title: Causation, correlation, and the limits of observational research
passages.text: One of the most fundamental distinctions in empirical science is between correlation and causation. Two variables may be statistically associated — tending to rise and fall together — without either causing the other. A classic illustration is the strong correlation between ice cream sales and drowning rates: both increase in summer, but neither causes the other; both are driven by the confounding variable of warm weather. In observational studies, where researchers record naturally occurring phenomena rather than manipulating variables in controlled conditions, the identification of genuine causal relationships is enormously challenging. The problem is that any observed association between an exposure and an outcome may reflect the effect of measured or unmeasured confounders — variables that are related to both exposure and outcome and distort the apparent association between them. Researchers employ various statistical techniques, such as multivariate regression analysis and propensity score matching, to control for known confounders, but unmeasured confounders remain an irreducible source of uncertainty. The randomised controlled trial (RCT) circumvents this problem by randomly assigning participants to exposed and unexposed groups, ensuring that — on average and across large samples — both measured and unmeasured confounders are distributed equally between groups. This allows causal inferences that observational designs cannot support. However, RCTs are frequently infeasible on ethical, practical, or financial grounds, particularly in epidemiology, economics, and social policy research, where researchers must rely on quasi-experimental methods that approximate but cannot fully replicate the logic of random assignment.

questions.q: What does the ice cream and drowning rate example illustrate in the passage?
options: The ethical problems of using observational data for policy decisions
How two variables can be statistically correlated without either causing the other
The difficulty of collecting accurate data in naturalistic settings
Why randomised controlled trials are the only valid form of scientific evidence
questions.answer: How two variables can be statistically correlated without either causing the other

questions.q: Why is identifying genuine causal relationships in observational studies particularly difficult?
options: Because researchers in observational studies do not use statistical methods to analyse their data
Because observed associations may reflect the influence of unmeasured confounders that distort the apparent relationship
Because observational studies are too small to detect statistically significant effects
Because participants in observational studies are aware of the researchers' hypotheses
questions.answer: Because observed associations may reflect the influence of unmeasured confounders that distort the apparent relationship

questions.q: What is the advantage of randomised controlled trials over observational studies for establishing causation?
options: They are always cheaper and faster to conduct than observational studies
Random assignment ensures that both measured and unmeasured confounders are distributed equally between groups
They eliminate the need for statistical analysis by directly observing cause and effect
They can be conducted in any research context without ethical constraints
questions.answer: Random assignment ensures that both measured and unmeasured confounders are distributed equally between groups

passages.title: Evidence-based policy and the translation of research into practice
passages.text: The evidence-based policy movement — which seeks to ground government decisions in the findings of rigorous empirical research rather than in ideology, tradition, or political interest — has transformed how many governments and international organisations approach policymaking. The underlying premise is straightforward: in a world of limited resources and complex problems, decisions about which interventions to implement should be informed by systematic evidence about what works, for whom, under what conditions, and at what cost. In practice, however, the relationship between research evidence and policy decisions is considerably more complex than the linear model of 'research produces knowledge, knowledge informs policy' suggests. Policy decisions occur in contested political environments where multiple interests and values compete, where the relevant research base is frequently incomplete or contradictory, and where decision-makers face time pressures that do not accommodate the pace of scientific enquiry. Furthermore, research findings generated in one context — a randomised trial conducted in urban schools in Massachusetts, for instance — may not generalise to very different contexts. The concept of external validity, or generalisability, is therefore critical: a finding that is internally valid — correctly identifying a causal relationship within a specific study — may nonetheless be of limited relevance to policy contexts that differ substantially in population characteristics, institutional capacity, or cultural context. The most honest and productive relationship between research and policy involves not the simple transfer of findings but an iterative dialogue in which researchers and policymakers together assess what the evidence can and cannot tell us about a specific decision.

questions.q: What is the core premise of the evidence-based policy movement?
options: That government decisions should be made by scientific experts rather than elected politicians
That decisions about which interventions to implement should be informed by systematic evidence about what works
That all policy interventions must be tested through randomised controlled trials before implementation
That quantitative evidence is always more reliable than qualitative experience in policy design
questions.answer: That decisions about which interventions to implement should be informed by systematic evidence about what works

questions.q: What does the passage identify as a limitation of the linear model of research-to-policy translation?
options: That research is always conducted too slowly to inform urgent policy decisions
That policy decisions occur in contested political environments where evidence competes with interests and values
That researchers lack the political skills needed to communicate their findings to policymakers
That governments are unwilling to fund research that might challenge existing policies
questions.answer: That policy decisions occur in contested political environments where evidence competes with interests and values

questions.q: Why is external validity particularly important in evidence-based policy?
options: Because it determines whether a study has been conducted according to ethical guidelines
Because internally valid findings from one context may not generalise to policy contexts with different characteristics
