Because diplomatic training deliberately cultivates these qualities as markers of professional sophistication
Because international law requires diplomatic communications to be open to multiple interpretations to avoid binding commitments
questions.answer: Because they are adaptations to an environment where clarity can be dangerous, precedents are binding, and ongoing relationships must be maintained

questions.q: What does the passage say is the actual communicative function of the formula 'both sides agreed to continue dialogue'?
options: To formally confirm that negotiations have produced a commitment to further engagement on both sides
To represent the absence of agreement as a form of progress, providing face-saving exits from deadlock
To signal to domestic audiences that their representatives have defended national interests effectively
To create a legally binding record of the parties' commitment to a peaceful resolution of their dispute
questions.answer: To represent the absence of agreement as a form of progress, providing face-saving exits from deadlock

questions.q: What social function does the passage attribute to diplomatic register that explicit language cannot serve?
options: Preventing leaks to the press by ensuring that the substance of negotiations cannot be easily understood by outsiders
Creating negotiating space by allowing parties to explore positions without committing to them and managing face threats
Establishing the procedural frameworks within which substantive negotiations can take place
Ensuring that the legal precision required for binding international agreements is maintained throughout the negotiating process
questions.answer: Creating negotiating space by allowing parties to explore positions without committing to them and managing face threats

passages.title: Metaphor as thought: the conceptual metaphor theory
passages.text: The publication of Lakoff and Johnson's Metaphors We Live By in 1980 represented a paradigm shift in the linguistics and philosophy of language by demonstrating that metaphor is not a decorative feature of literary language but the fundamental cognitive mechanism by which abstract concepts are structured and understood. On the classical view, metaphor is a figure of speech in which one thing is described in terms of another for rhetorical effect — a departure from the literal, proper use of language that is optional, explicable by paraphrase, and characteristic of poetic rather than ordinary discourse. Lakoff and Johnson showed that this view is wrong in every essential respect: ordinary conceptual thought is saturated with metaphorical structure that is not optional, cannot be fully paraphrased in literal terms, and is not the product of a conscious rhetorical decision but of the way abstract domains are cognitively constituted. We do not merely talk about argument in terms of war — 'I defended my position', 'her claims were indefensible', 'he attacked every weak point in my argument' — we actually think about it that way, and this structuring determines what we notice, what moves are available to us, and what we can understand. The same is true of time ('time is money'), the mind ('the mind is a machine'), and ideas ('ideas are food', 'I can't digest all this at once', 'let me chew on that'). Changing the conceptual metaphor that structures a domain changes what is thinkable within it: describing immigration as an 'invasion' activates a military frame with its associated implications of threat, defence, and the legitimacy of force, while describing it as a 'flow' activates a hydraulic frame that implies management rather than confrontation.

questions.q: What does the passage identify as the classical view of metaphor that Lakoff and Johnson challenged?
options: That metaphor is universal across human languages and therefore reflects deep cognitive structures
That metaphor is a decorative figure of speech, departure from literal language, optional and characteristic of poetry
That metaphor operates primarily through analogical reasoning based on structural similarities between domains
That metaphor is primarily a device for communicating emotional states that cannot be expressed in literal terms
questions.answer: That metaphor is a decorative figure of speech, departure from literal language, optional and characteristic of poetry

questions.q: What does the 'argument is war' example demonstrate about conceptual metaphors according to the passage?
options: That English is a more aggressive language than other languages because of this particular conceptual structure
That the metaphor structures how we actually think about argument — what moves are available, what we notice, what we understand
That conceptual metaphors are most visible when they are extended across a long series of linguistic expressions
That the rhetorical framing of disagreements as battles inevitably escalates conflict rather than enabling its resolution
questions.answer: That the metaphor structures how we actually think about argument — what moves are available, what we notice, what we understand

questions.q: How does the passage illustrate the political stakes of conceptual metaphor choice?
options: By noting that politicians consistently use more metaphorical language than other professionals because it is more persuasive
By showing how 'invasion' versus 'flow' metaphors for immigration activate different cognitive frames with different implications for policy
By arguing that conceptual metaphors are more powerful in spoken than written discourse because of their emotional resonance
By demonstrating that the same conceptual metaphor can support diametrically opposed political positions depending on the context
questions.answer: By showing how 'invasion' versus 'flow' metaphors for immigration activate different cognitive frames with different implications for policy

passages.title: Collocation, idiom, and the limits of compositionality
passages.text: The principle of compositionality — the assumption that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and the rules by which they are combined — is one of the foundational principles of formal linguistics and provides the theoretical basis for grammar as a generative system. It is also, for the pragmatic purposes of language acquisition and use, significantly misleading. A very large proportion of authentic native speech consists not of novel sentences generated from scratch by the application of compositional rules, but of pre-fabricated multiword units — collocations, idioms, phrasal verbs, discourse markers, and other chunks — that are stored and retrieved as single items rather than assembled from their parts. The pedagogical implication is that vocabulary instruction cannot be limited to teaching single words and grammar instruction to teaching compositional rules: the learner who knows the meanings of 'make' and 'sense' may still be unable to use 'make sense' correctly, because 'make' selects specific nominal complements that cannot be predicted from its general semantics. Similarly, the learner who understands 'kick' and 'bucket' individually cannot derive the idiom 'kick the bucket' from those meanings, because the idiomatic meaning is stored as a separate lexical entry that supersedes the compositional meaning. Corpus linguistics, which analyses large databases of authentic language use, has quantified the scale of this phenomenon: studies consistently show that a significant proportion — some researchers suggest the majority — of running text in authentic speech and writing can be accounted for by recurrent multiword patterns rather than novel compositional generation. The native speaker's advantage over the advanced learner therefore lies not primarily in grammatical knowledge but in the extent and accessibility of their stored chunk inventory.

questions.q: What does the passage identify as misleading about the principle of compositionality for practical language acquisition?
options: That it ignores the role of context in determining meaning, which is more important than compositional rules
That a large proportion of authentic speech consists of pre-fabricated multiword units stored as single items rather than assembled compositionally
That compositional rules are too complex for most language learners to master explicitly without specialised linguistic training
That the principle applies to formal written language but not to the informal spoken language that most learners need to acquire
questions.answer: That a large proportion of authentic speech consists of pre-fabricated multiword units stored as single items rather than assembled compositionally

questions.q: How does the passage use the 'make sense' example to illustrate the limits of compositional vocabulary learning?
options: To show that phrasal expressions have different grammatical properties from single words and must be taught as a separate category
To demonstrate that knowing individual word meanings is insufficient if the learner does not also know the specific collocational patterns
To argue that collocation patterns are more important than grammar rules in determining whether a sentence sounds natural
To illustrate that idioms are always less precise than compositional expressions and should be avoided in formal writing
questions.answer: To demonstrate that knowing individual word meanings is insufficient if the learner does not also know the specific collocational patterns

questions.q: What finding from corpus linguistics does the passage cite, and what implication does it draw from it?
options: That idioms are more frequent in spoken than written language, implying they should be prioritised in oral communication training
That a significant proportion of authentic text can be accounted for by recurrent multiword patterns, implying native advantage lies in stored chunk inventory rather than grammatical knowledge
That collocation errors are the most common type of error in advanced learner writing, implying they should be the focus of error correction
That formal registers contain fewer idiomatic expressions than informal ones, implying register instruction should focus on collocational rather than idiomatic knowledge
questions.answer: That a significant proportion of authentic text can be accounted for by recurrent multiword patterns, implying native advantage lies in stored chunk inventory rather than grammatical knowledge

passages.title: Connotation, register, and the politics of word choice
passages.text: The distinction between denotation and connotation is one of the most practically important in the analysis of how language shapes thought and social reality, yet it is consistently underestimated in language education, which tends to treat near-synonyms as interchangeable once the denotative core is established. Words that share a denotative meaning can differ radically in their connotative associations — the social, emotional, and evaluative meanings that cluster around a lexical item as a result of its patterns of use in the culture. These connotative associations are not accidents or decoration: they encode the value judgements, social hierarchies, and ideological commitments of the communities that use the language, and they are reproduced and reinforced every time a word is used. The choice between 'freedom fighter' and 'terrorist' to describe the same individual is not a semantic question answerable by reference to facts about that individual's actions; it is a political choice that encodes a prior judgement about the legitimacy of those actions that then frames all subsequent evaluation. Similarly, the choice between 'illegal alien', 'undocumented immigrant', and 'asylum seeker' to describe the same person does not merely reflect different factual emphases but activates different frames — legal/criminal, administrative/regulatory, humanitarian — that predispose the listener toward different policy responses. The advanced language user must therefore develop what might be called connotative literacy: the ability to recognise the evaluative loading of words, to distinguish between denotative precision and connotative neutrality, and to make deliberate rather than inadvertent choices about the ideological commitments encoded in every lexical selection.

questions.q: What claim does the passage make about the practical importance of the denotation/connotation distinction?
options: That connotation is the primary vehicle of emotional communication while denotation handles factual content
That near-synonyms cannot be treated as interchangeable once the denotative core is established because connotative associations encode value judgements
That connotation is more culturally variable than denotation and therefore more difficult to acquire as a second language learner
That the distinction is most important in literary analysis and less relevant to everyday professional or political communication
questions.answer: That near-synonyms cannot be treated as interchangeable once the denotative core is established because connotative associations encode value judgements

questions.q: How does the passage use the 'freedom fighter/terrorist' example?
options: To illustrate how the same action can be described in factually accurate but evaluatively neutral terms
To show that the choice between the two terms is a political one encoding prior judgements about legitimacy that frame all subsequent evaluation
To demonstrate that journalists must use legally precise terminology when reporting on political violence
To argue that the connotations of politically charged terms change over time as the historical meaning of events is reassessed
questions.answer: To show that the choice between the two terms is a political one encoding prior judgements about legitimacy that frame all subsequent evaluation

questions.q: What does the passage mean by 'connotative literacy' as a competency for advanced language users?
options: The ability to use the full range of emotional and aesthetic connotations of words in literary and creative writing
The ability to recognise the evaluative loading of words and make deliberate rather than inadvertent choices about ideological commitments
The ability to produce and interpret texts in a wide variety of registers from academic to colloquial without loss of connotative precision
The ability to distinguish between words with positive and negative connotations and to use positive connotations in persuasive contexts
questions.answer: The ability to recognise the evaluative loading of words and make deliberate rather than inadvertent choices about ideological commitments

passages.title: Linguistic mediation and the ethics of translation
passages.text: Translation — the most visible form of linguistic mediation — makes visible, in concentrated form, the dilemmas that all mediated communication faces but that intralinguistic communication can more easily paper over. The translator must navigate between two competing obligations: fidelity to the source text's meaning, tone, cultural context, and formal properties; and accessibility to the target text's audience, whose linguistic resources, cultural references, and reading conventions may differ radically from those of the source culture. These obligations are not merely in tension but are in principle irreconcilable: a translation that maximises fidelity to the source will be culturally foreign to the target audience; a translation that maximises accessibility to the target audience will inevitably domesticate — and thereby distort — the source. The domesticating translation makes the foreign familiar; the foreignising translation keeps it strange. Neither is neutral: both make choices that have ideological implications about which culture's norms should take precedence and which audience's expectations should be satisfied. This dilemma is not uniquely the translator's: the interpreter who renders a technical document for a lay audience, the mediator who conveys one party's position to another across a cultural divide, the executive who reformulates a policy decision for different stakeholder groups — all face versions of the same choice between fidelity and accessibility, and all make, whether consciously or not, choices that shape not just how the message is received but what message is ultimately received.

questions.q: What does the passage identify as the two competing and in principle irreconcilable obligations of the translator?
options: The obligation to preserve the formal properties of the source text and the obligation to produce a target text that reads naturally
Fidelity to the source text's meaning and cultural context, and accessibility to the target audience's linguistic resources and conventions
Obligation to the author of the source text and obligation to the publisher who has commissioned the translation
Accuracy in conveying factual information and faithfulness in conveying the author's emotional and aesthetic intentions
questions.answer: Fidelity to the source text's meaning and cultural context, and accessibility to the target audience's linguistic resources and conventions

questions.q: What does the passage say about the ideological implications of choosing between domesticating and foreignising translation strategies?
options: That foreignising translation is always superior because it respects the source culture's integrity and resists cultural imperialism
That both strategies make choices with ideological implications about which culture's norms should take precedence
That domesticating translation is preferred in commercial contexts while foreignising is preferred in academic and literary translation
That the choice between strategies should be determined by the nature of the text rather than the translator's cultural or political commitments
questions.answer: That both strategies make choices with ideological implications about which culture's norms should take precedence

questions.q: How does the passage extend the translation dilemma beyond the professional translator?
options: By arguing that all speakers of a second language face the same choices as translators when communicating across cultural boundaries
By showing that mediators, interpreters of technical documents, and executives reformulating for stakeholders all face versions of the fidelity/accessibility choice
By noting that the dilemma was identified by literary theorists but applies equally to legal and diplomatic translation
By suggesting that digital translation tools will eventually resolve the dilemma by making fully literal translation accessible to target audiences
questions.answer: By showing that mediators, interpreters of technical documents, and executives reformulating for stakeholders all face versions of the fidelity/accessibility choice

passages.title: Discourse coherence and the art of synthesis
passages.text: The capacity to write coherently — to produce a text that a reader can process as a unified, structured argument rather than a sequence of disconnected observations — is among the most valued and most difficult of academic competencies, and its analysis reveals that it depends on a set of skills quite distinct from those required for grammatical accuracy at the sentence level. A collection of perfectly grammatical sentences does not automatically constitute a coherent text: coherence is a property of the relationship between sentences, not of any individual sentence, and it is achieved through a combination of mechanisms that operate at the lexical, syntactic, and discursive levels simultaneously. At the lexical level, cohesion is created through the repetition of key terms, the use of synonyms and hyperonyms to refer back to previously introduced concepts, and the deployment of pronouns and demonstratives as anaphoric reference chains. At the discursive level, coherence requires that ideas be ordered according to a logic that the reader can follow — typically moving from given to new information within sentences, from general to specific within paragraphs, and from setup to development to conclusion across a text as a whole. The hardest challenge in academic writing is not to express individual ideas clearly but to synthesise multiple sources and perspectives into a structured argument that does justice to their complexity while maintaining a through-line that the reader can follow. This requires what might be called macrostructural competence: the ability to see and shape the overall architecture of a text, not just to manage its local linguistic features.

questions.q: What distinction does the passage draw between grammatical accuracy at the sentence level and discourse coherence?
options: That grammatical accuracy is a necessary condition for discourse coherence but not sufficient — coherence depends on relationships between sentences
That grammatical accuracy is more important in formal academic writing while discourse coherence matters more in spoken communication
That native speakers achieve discourse coherence intuitively while grammatical accuracy requires explicit instruction for all learners
That discourse coherence is a property of whole texts while grammatical accuracy can be assessed at any level from word to paragraph
questions.answer: That grammatical accuracy is a necessary condition for discourse coherence but not sufficient — coherence depends on relationships between sentences

questions.q: What does the passage identify as the mechanisms of cohesion at the lexical level?
options: Correct subject-verb agreement, appropriate tense sequence, and consistent use of articles and determiners
Repetition of key terms, use of synonyms and hyperonyms, and pronouns and demonstratives as anaphoric reference chains
Appropriate use of discourse markers like 'however', 'therefore', 'moreover', and 'in contrast'
Clear topic sentences at the beginning of each paragraph that introduce the main idea to be developed
questions.answer: Repetition of key terms, use of synonyms and hyperonyms, and pronouns and demonstratives as anaphoric reference chains

questions.q: What does the passage call the highest-level competency required in academic writing and how does it define it?
options: Lexical sophistication: the ability to choose between near-synonyms to achieve the most precise connotative effect
Macrostructural competence: the ability to see and shape the overall architecture of a text rather than just managing local features
Synthesising competence: the ability to combine the arguments of multiple sources without losing the individual source's contribution
Pragmatic competence: the ability to calibrate the directness and formality of academic writing to different disciplinary norms
questions.answer: Macrostructural competence: the ability to see and shape the overall architecture of a text rather than just managing local features

passages.title: The C2 speaker: language as inhabitation
passages.text: The distinction between an advanced language learner and a genuinely proficient speaker is not primarily a matter of the size of one's vocabulary, the accuracy of one's grammar, or even the breadth of one's pragmatic competence — though all of these are necessary conditions for proficiency. It is a matter of the relationship the speaker has with the language: whether they use it as a tool that requires effort to wield or whether they inhabit it as a medium that they think in, feel in, and orient toward the world through. This distinction is not merely phenomenological but has practical consequences. The language user for whom English is a tool — however sophisticated a tool — must allocate cognitive resources to language production that the truly proficient speaker can direct to the communicative task itself: to the argument being constructed, the relationship being managed, the text being written. Automaticity — the unconscious execution of complex linguistic operations without deliberate attention — releases the processing capacity that is then available for the higher-order cognitive work that sophisticated communication demands. The C2 descriptor in the Common European Framework of Reference captures this not in terms of any specific grammatical or lexical competency but in terms of the speaker's ability to express themselves 'spontaneously, very fluently and precisely, differentiating finer shades of meaning even in more complex situations'. The 'finer shades of meaning' that the C2 speaker controls — the difference between 'persuade' and 'convince', between 'disinterested' and 'uninterested', between 'infer' and 'imply', between a comma splice and a deliberate stylistic choice — are not cataloguable in any finite list. They are the product of a relationship with the language that has been built through sustained engagement with its full range of authentic uses.

questions.q: What does the passage identify as the fundamental distinction between advanced learners and genuinely proficient speakers?
options: The size and range of their productive vocabulary across formal and informal registers
Whether they use language as a tool requiring effort or inhabit it as a medium they think, feel, and orient through
The degree to which they have internalised the grammar rules of the language at a conscious, explicable level
Their ability to produce error-free language under pressure and in real-time communicative situations
questions.answer: Whether they use language as a tool requiring effort or inhabit it as a medium they think, feel, and orient through

questions.q: What practical consequence does the passage draw from the distinction between using language as a tool versus inhabiting it?
options: That the habitual user is more creative in their language use because they are not constrained by explicit rules
That the tool-user must allocate cognitive resources to production that the proficient speaker can direct to the communicative task itself
That the proficient speaker has greater awareness of their own linguistic choices because they make them consciously
That habitation requires greater exposure to the target culture than to the target language itself
questions.answer: That the tool-user must allocate cognitive resources to production that the proficient speaker can direct to the communicative task itself

questions.q: How does the passage characterise the 'finer shades of meaning' that define C2 competence?
options: As a specific list of advanced vocabulary and grammar items that can be taught systematically in a C2 preparation course
As the product of a relationship with the language built through sustained engagement with its full authentic range — not cataloguable in a finite list
As primarily pragmatic distinctions about appropriateness across contexts rather than semantic distinctions within a single context
As the ability to use literary and rhetorical devices that are characteristically absent from the language of non-native speakers
questions.answer: As the product of a relationship with the language built through sustained engagement with its full authentic range — not cataloguable in a finite list
